article.body:
We are investigating what makes a physical system truly remember its past. Consider a computer hard drive versus a pebble on a beach. One holds onto meaningful data while the other simply decays. [1, 3] To understand this, our group studied the rules of causal memory. A system only acts as a memory if it can accurately predict something about its own future. [1, 3] We found that the reliability of this memory is fundamentally limited by the energy cost of observing that system. [2] Better prediction often requires more energy to sustain. We analyzed how one-way interactions between components help control how much energy a system wastes while maintaining its internal records. [4] Next, we looked at how an internal memory becomes objective, meaning independent observers can agree on what it says. Imagine you have a secret, and you make a thousand copies of the note to throw into the wind. [5] Even if someone catches only one, they have the same information as everyone else. [6, 8] This broadcasting works until the environment starts scrambling the data. If the environment scrambles information faster than a system can share it, that history becomes lost. [7] Finally, we studied chemical networks that act like self-sustaining loops. These are groups of reactions that keep producing their own ingredients, known as autocatalytic networks. [10, 11] We found that mathematical maps of these chemical balances dictate which networks persist. [9, 12] While these loops can hold history, they are not necessarily evolving. We still do not know at what precise threshold a system stops simply repeating its past and starts creating a lineage that can adapt. [9, 12]

Summary

Our group examined how systems keep records of the past. We found that storing a reliable memory requires energy. We also studied how systems broadcast information so that many people can see the same facts, even when the environment is jumbled. Finally, we looked at chemical loops that act like a self-sustaining history. While these systems can remember their own story, we still do not know exactly when they cross the line into becoming capable of evolving.
article.lede: Our research explores how physical systems hold onto their history, how information becomes publicly available, and whether chemical loops can cross the line into genuine evolution.
article.lens: This editorial sequence maps the operational constraints of memory, from energy-intensive physical prediction to the redundant broadcast of objective records, and finally to the threshold of heredity in chemical networks.
article.title: Mapping the Boundaries of Memory

To this end, accurate prediction of thermodynamic, transport, structural, and interfacial properties is important for overcoming engineering challenges across the entire H<sub>2</sub> value chain. Experimental measurements, despite being the traditional way of obtaining these properties, can be limited by the distinctive nature of H<sub>2</sub>, harsh operating conditions, safety constraints, and extensive parameter spaces. Free from such limitations, classical molecular simulations, in the general frameworks of Monte Carlo and Molecular Dynamics, provide an optimal balance between computational efficiency and accuracy, bridging the gap between quantum mechanical calculations and macro-scale modeling. This review also systematically covers molecular simulation methods and force fields for computing key properties of H<sub>2</sub> systems, such as phase and adsorption equilibria and transport coefficients. Beyond property prediction, we explore how molecular simulation reveals fundamental mechanisms governing hydrate formation and dissociation, membrane permeations, and H<sub>2</sub> embrittlement.
